title: A real no-solution proof cannot be moved to the complex numbers

original_problem.statement: Solve z^2+1=0 for the admissible number system, initially the reals.
original_problem.goal: Find the complete solution set of z^2+1=0 for the current admissible domain.

conditions.description: The number system admissible for z.

assumptions.description: The admissible number system has a real order structure making z^2>=0 a theorem.

methods.name: Real-order nonnegativity argument
methods.description: Rearrange to z^2=-1, apply z^2>=0, and conclude no solutions.

correct_steps.explanation: Pure rearrangement; valid in both the real and complex numbers.
Apply the real theorem that every square is nonnegative.
Since -1<0, the equation has no admissible solutions.

allowed_perturbations.description: Widen the admissible domain to the complex numbers.
Restrict the admissible domain to the nonnegative reals.

expected_failure_mechanisms: Over the complex numbers, z^2+1=(z-i)(z+i)=0 has solutions {-i, i}; the real order theorem z^2>=0 does not apply because C has no order structure.

verification_rules.description: Pure rearrangement, valid on either domain.
Check whether the real-order nonnegativity theorem applies on the current domain.
Independently solve the original equation and compare to the claimed empty set.

explanation_fragments.text: The complex numbers have no order structure, so z^2>=0 is not a theorem there. Factoring z^2+1=(z-i)(z+i) gives the complete solution set {-i, i}; the real no-solution argument does not transfer.

review.basis: Independently approved by Claude Code, acting as implementer/reviewer under explicit user authorization after Codex hit a usage limit: hand-verified z^2+1=(z-i)(z+i), both roots check, and the real/nonnegative-real domains stay empty.
